lines.display: Hello! Today, let's get to know our own home, the planet **Earth**.
We will see what covers Earth, and where it sits among the planets.
We will learn why living things can live here, and Earth's real shape.
Then we will see how Earth's spin gives us day and night.
We will even meet an old clock that reads the Sun's shadow!
Last, we will follow Earth around the Sun, and find what brings the seasons.
Let's begin with the name **Earth**.
The name Earth comes from **Old English**.
Old English is the English that people spoke very long ago.
In Old English, the word meant **soil**, or **ground**.
It meant the ground under our feet!

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Where the Name Comes From

lines.display: You already know that Earth is the planet we live on.
A **planet** is a huge world that goes around the Sun.
Earth is one of these planets.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: What Is a Planet?

lines.display: Let's find Earth's place among the planets.
Start with the planet nearest the Sun.
Then count the planets as you move away from the Sun.
Earth comes third.
So Earth is the **third planet from the Sun**.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Earth Comes Third

lines.display: We call the Sun and its planets the **solar system**.
Earth is special in the solar system.
To see why, we need two words: **liquid** and **surface**.

conceptGroup.goal: Find the one thing only Earth has in the solar system
conceptGroup.title: What makes Earth special?

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: What Makes Earth Special?

lines.display: You know that water can be solid ice, or vapour in the air.
Water can also flow.
Water that flows is **liquid** water.
It is the water we pour into a glass and drink.

conceptGroup.goal: Find the one thing only Earth has in the solar system
conceptGroup.title: What makes Earth special?

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Liquid Water

lines.display: We live on the outside of Earth.
We call this outside its **surface**.
The ground under your feet is part of Earth's surface.

conceptGroup.goal: Find the one thing only Earth has in the solar system
conceptGroup.title: What makes Earth special?

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Earth's Surface

lines.display: Now here is what makes Earth special.
No other planet in the solar system has **liquid water** on its surface.
Only Earth has flowing water on its outside.

conceptGroup.goal: Find the one thing only Earth has in the solar system
conceptGroup.title: What makes Earth special?

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Only Earth Has Flowing Water

question.prompt: What makes Earth special in the solar system?

options.text: It goes around the Sun.
It has liquid water on its surface.
It is the only planet.

hint.display: Remember, every planet goes around the Sun.

grading.correctAnswerText: It has liquid water on its surface.
grading.reason: Yes! Only Earth has liquid water on its surface.

conceptGroup.goal: Find the one thing only Earth has in the solar system
conceptGroup.title: What makes Earth special?

question.prompt: Which of these sentences are true?

options.text: Ice is liquid water.
Water that flows is liquid water.
Vapour in the air is liquid water.
We live on Earth's surface.

hint.display: Ask yourself: can it flow?

grading.correctAnswerText: Water that flows is liquid water.; We live on Earth's surface.
grading.reason: Great thinking! Ice and vapour are water too, but they are not liquid.

conceptGroup.goal: Find the one thing only Earth has in the solar system
conceptGroup.title: What makes Earth special?

lines.display: Earth has a lot of this water.
About **71%** of Earth's surface is water.
The other **29%** is land.
Let's see what these two numbers tell us.

conceptGroup.goal: Find out what 71% and 29% tell us about Earth's surface
conceptGroup.title: 71% water, 29% land

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: How Much Water?

lines.display: What does 71% mean?
The sign **%** means “out of every 100”.
So we read 71% as “71 out of every 100 parts”.

conceptGroup.goal: Find out what 71% and 29% tell us about Earth's surface
conceptGroup.title: 71% water, 29% land

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: What Does 71% Mean?

lines.display: Imagine we split Earth's whole surface into 100 equal parts.
**71** of these parts are water.
The other **29** parts are land.
Together, 71 and 29 make 100.
So the water and the land together make the whole surface.

conceptGroup.goal: Find out what 71% and 29% tell us about Earth's surface
conceptGroup.title: 71% water, 29% land

visual.title: Split Into 100 Parts
visual.description: Earth's whole surface as a 10 x 10 grid of 100 equal squares: 71 water squares in blue, 29 land squares in brown, and 71 + 29 = 100.

lines.display: Now compare the two numbers.
71 is much bigger than 29.
So water covers **most** of Earth's surface.

conceptGroup.goal: Find out what 71% and 29% tell us about Earth's surface
conceptGroup.title: 71% water, 29% land

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Water Covers Most

question.prompt: 71% means 71 out of every ___ parts.

hint.display: Remember: we split Earth's whole surface into equal parts.

grading.reason: Yes! The percent sign means out of every 100.

conceptGroup.goal: Find out what 71% and 29% tell us about Earth's surface
conceptGroup.title: 71% water, 29% land

options.text: Yes. People live on land, so land covers most.
Yes. 29 is bigger than 71.
No. 71 out of every 100 parts are water.

hint.display: Compare the two numbers, 71 and 29.

grading.reason: Well done! 71 is much bigger than 29, so water covers most.

conceptGroup.goal: Find out what 71% and 29% tell us about Earth's surface
conceptGroup.title: 71% water, 29% land

lines.display: Where is all this water?
Earth has water in three forms.
**Liquid** water fills the oceans, seas, rivers and lakes.
**Water vapour** is in the air.
And **ice** sits on snow-capped mountains and in glaciers.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Water in Three Forms

lines.display: **Water vapour** is water in the air as a gas.
We cannot see it, but it is there.
**Snow-capped** mountains have snow on top, like a cap.
The high Himalayas are snow-capped.
A **glacier** is a huge mass of ice, much bigger than a house.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Vapour, Snow and Glaciers

lines.display: Earth has many kinds of land, too.
There are high **mountains**.
There are deep **valleys**, the low land between mountains.
There are **plains**, wide and flat land.
There are **plateaus**, high land with a flat top.
And there are **arid deserts**.
**Arid** means very dry.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Many Kinds of Land

lines.display: You met some of these in the chapters on Northern and Southern India.
Remember the **Himalayas**, the **Northern Plains**, the **Thar Desert** and the **Deccan Plateau**?
Each one is a kind of land from our list.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Land You Have Met

question.prompt:
True or false?

All of Earth's water is in oceans and rivers.

options.text: True
False

hint.display: Think of all three forms of water.

grading.correctAnswerText: False
grading.reason: Right, it is false! Earth also has vapour in the air, and ice.

question.prompt: Which of these are kinds of land?

options.text: A glacier
The Thar Desert
The Deccan Plateau
Water vapour
The Himalayas

hint.display: Ask: is it land, or is it a form of water?

grading.correctAnswerText: The Thar Desert; The Deccan Plateau; The Himalayas
grading.reason: Well done! A desert, a plateau and mountains are all kinds of land.

lines.display: We have seen what covers Earth: water and land.
Now let's look far into space, at the whole **solar system**.
The **Sun** is in the middle.
**Eight planets** go around it.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Out Into Space

lines.display: In order from the Sun, first come **Mercury**, **Venus**, **Earth** and **Mars**.
Then come **Jupiter**, **Saturn**, **Uranus** and **Neptune**.
See? Earth is **third**, just as we learned.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: The Planets in Order

lines.display: Of these eight planets, **Jupiter** is the biggest.
**Mercury** is the smallest.
And **Saturn** has rings around it.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Biggest, Smallest, Rings

question.prompt: Of the eight planets, ___ is the biggest.

options.text: Mercury
Earth
Jupiter

hint.display: It comes just after Mars, going out from the Sun.

grading.correctAnswerText: Jupiter
grading.reason: Yes! Jupiter is the biggest, and Mercury is the smallest.

question.prompt: Earth is the third planet from the Sun. What does this tell us?

options.text: Two planets are nearer the Sun than Earth.
Earth is the third biggest planet.
The Sun is the first planet.

hint.display: Count the planets, starting from the one nearest the Sun.

grading.correctAnswerText: Two planets are nearer the Sun than Earth.
grading.reason: Great thinking! Mercury and Venus are nearer the Sun than Earth.

lines.display: Now, which of these planets has living things?
Till now, people have found living things only on Earth.
So Earth is the only planet **known to have life**.
Why is Earth such a good home for living things?
There are two reasons.

conceptGroup.goal: Find the two reasons living things can live on Earth
conceptGroup.title: Why Earth is a good home

lines.display: The first reason is Earth's distance from the Sun.
Earth is about **150 million km** away from the Sun.
This is **the right distance** for life.
At this distance, Earth gets the heat and light that life needs.
But it does not get too much.

conceptGroup.goal: Find the two reasons living things can live on Earth
conceptGroup.title: Why Earth is a good home

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Reason One: The Right Distance

cards.title: Too Hot, Too Cold, Just Right

lines.display: Here is a way to picture it.
Think of the space around the Sun in three parts.
The part close to the Sun is too hot for life.
The part far from the Sun is too cold for life.
The part in between is just right.
Earth sits in this just-right part.

conceptGroup.goal: Find the two reasons living things can live on Earth
conceptGroup.title: Why Earth is a good home

visual.title: Too Hot, Too Cold, Just Right
visual.description: The space around the Sun in three parts, too hot near the Sun, too cold far away, just right in between, with Earth in the just-right part.

interactive.label: Move the planet nearer to or farther from the Sun

cards.title: Reason Two: A Layer of Air

lines.display: The second reason is air.
A **layer of air** covers Earth from all sides.
Remember the chapter Air We Breathe?
Living things need air to live.
Earth's layer of air gives living things the air they need.

conceptGroup.goal: Find the two reasons living things can live on Earth
conceptGroup.title: Why Earth is a good home

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Reason Two: A Layer of Air

lines.display: So Earth is at the right distance from the Sun.
And it has a layer of air.
That is why Earth is such a good home for life.

conceptGroup.goal: Find the two reasons living things can live on Earth
conceptGroup.title: Why Earth is a good home

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: A Good Home for Life

question.prompt:
True or false?

A planet close to the Sun is too hot for life.

options.text: True
False

hint.display: Think about the three parts of space around the Sun.

grading.correctAnswerText: True
grading.reason: Yes, it is true! Earth sits in the just-right part instead.

conceptGroup.goal: Find the two reasons living things can live on Earth
conceptGroup.title: Why Earth is a good home

question.prompt: A planet is at the right distance from the Sun. But it has no layer of air. Which of these are true about it?

options.text: It is too hot for life.
It gets the heat and light that life needs.
Living things could not get the air they need.
It is a good home for life.

hint.display: Ask: does this planet give living things everything they need?

grading.correctAnswerText: It gets the heat and light that life needs.; Living things could not get the air they need.
grading.reason: Well done! Without air, even the right distance is not enough.

conceptGroup.goal: Find the two reasons living things can live on Earth
conceptGroup.title: Why Earth is a good home

lines.display: Earth is our home, but what shape is it?
Is it really round?
Look around you.
A big field, a long road and the sea all look flat.
So, long ago, people believed that Earth was **flat**.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: What Shape Is Earth?

lines.display: Sailors long ago were afraid to sail too far.
They thought their ship would fall off Earth's edge.
But some brave sailors kept sailing for a very long time.
They never reached an edge.
In the end, they came back to the same place they started from!
Today, a plane can fly around Earth in about two days!

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Brave Sailors

lines.display: How could the sailors come back to their start?
Here is a way to see it.
Picture an ant on an orange.
The ant walks straight ahead and never turns.
After a while, it comes back to the spot where it began.
The sailors did the same thing on Earth.
This can only happen on a round Earth.

visual.title: An Ant on an Orange
visual.description: An ant walking straight ahead round an orange, never turning, and arriving back at its start flag.

lines.display: Now, what does “round” mean here?
You might think round means flat and round, like a coin.
But a ball is round too.
Let's see the difference.

conceptGroup.goal: Find out which kind of round Earth is
conceptGroup.title: Round like a coin, or a ball?

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: What Does Round Mean?

lines.display: Hold a one-rupee coin and an orange in front of your eyes.
Turn each one slowly, all the way round.
The orange looks round from every side.
The coin looks round only from the front.
From the side, the coin looks like a thin line.
So the coin is flat and round.
The orange is round like a ball.

conceptGroup.goal: Find out which kind of round Earth is
conceptGroup.title: Round like a coin, or a ball?

visual.title: A Coin and an Orange
visual.description: A coin and an orange turned slowly side by side: from the side the coin is a thin line, the orange is still round.

interactive.label: Move the dot to turn the coin and the orange

cards.title: Which Kind of Round Is Earth?

lines.display: Which kind of round is Earth?
Think of the ant again.
On a flat coin, the ant walks straight and soon reaches the edge.
On a ball, it never reaches an edge.
It comes back to its start.
The sailors came back to their start too.
So Earth is round like a ball, not flat like a coin.

conceptGroup.goal: Find out which kind of round Earth is
conceptGroup.title: Round like a coin, or a ball?

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Which Kind of Round Is Earth?

question.prompt: Which kind of round is Earth?

options.text: Flat and round, like a coin
Round like a ball

hint.display: Think of the ant: does it reach an edge?

grading.correctAnswerText: Round like a ball
grading.reason: Yes! Earth is round like a ball, not flat like a coin.

conceptGroup.goal: Find out which kind of round Earth is
conceptGroup.title: Round like a coin, or a ball?

question.prompt: Which of these show that Earth is round like a ball?

options.text: Some sailors kept sailing and came back to their start.
A big field looks flat.
People long ago believed Earth was flat.
The sailors never reached an edge.

hint.display: A thing can look flat and still be round.

grading.correctAnswerText: Some sailors kept sailing and came back to their start.; The sailors never reached an edge.
grading.reason: Great thinking! The sailors came back to their start, so Earth is round.

conceptGroup.goal: Find out which kind of round Earth is
conceptGroup.title: Round like a coin, or a ball?

lines.display: We call a ball shape a **sphere**.
**Spherical** means shaped like a ball.
So we can say Earth is spherical, round like a ball.

conceptGroup.goal: Find out which kind of round Earth is
conceptGroup.title: Round like a coin, or a ball?

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: A Sphere

lines.display: Today, we can even see Earth's shape for ourselves.
Cameras in outer space have taken photographs of Earth.
**Outer space** is the huge space far above Earth's layer of air.
These photographs show Earth from many different sides.
Each one shows a round Earth.
None of them shows a thin line.
So Earth really is round like a ball.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Photographs From Space

lines.display: But look closely.
Earth is not a perfect ball.
It is a little squashed at the top and bottom, like an orange.
But it still looks round from every side.
It is not flat at all.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Not a Perfect Ball

lines.display: We call this shape an **oblate spheroid**.
“Spheroid” means almost a sphere.
“Oblate” means a little squashed at the top and bottom.
An oblate spheroid is Earth's **true shape**.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: An Oblate Spheroid

question.prompt:
True or false?

Earth is a perfect ball.

options.text: True
False

hint.display: Look closely at Earth's top and bottom.

grading.correctAnswerText: False
grading.reason: Right, it is false! Earth is a little squashed at the top and bottom.

question.prompt: Rohan hears that Earth is a little squashed. He says it is flat like a coin. Which of these show he is wrong?

options.text: From the side, Earth looks like a thin line.
Photographs from space show a round Earth.
Oblate means flat like a coin.
Earth is squashed only a little, like an orange.
Earth still looks round from every side.

hint.display: Think of an orange: squashed a little, but still round.

grading.correctAnswerText: Photographs from space show a round Earth.; Earth is squashed only a little, like an orange.; Earth still looks round from every side.
grading.reason: Well done! An oblate spheroid is almost a ball, not a coin.

lines.display: Our ball-shaped Earth is never still.
It moves in two ways.
It spins, and it travels around the Sun.
We call the spinning **rotation**.
We call the trip around the Sun **revolution**.
Let's learn about rotation first.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Earth Moves in Two Ways

lines.display: Every spinning thing turns around its middle.
Stand a bangle on the floor, on its edge.
Spin it with your fingers, like you spin a coin.
It turns round and round its middle.
Now look at its middle.
It is empty: only air, nothing to touch.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Spin a Bangle

lines.display: Imagine a straight line from the bangle's top down to the floor.
This line goes through the empty middle.
The bangle turns around this line.
We cannot see this line.
We can only imagine it.
So we call it an **imaginary line**.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: An Imaginary Line

lines.display: This imaginary line is the **axis**.
An **axis** is an imaginary line through the middle of a spinning thing.
The spinning thing turns around it.
A ball spinning on a table does the same.
It turns around its own axis.
And there is no stick inside the ball.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: The Axis

lines.display: Earth has an axis too.
It is an imaginary line through Earth's middle, from top to bottom.
Earth's axis is slightly **tilted**.
**Tilted** means leaning a little.
Think of a pencil in a glass, leaning a little to one side.
We will need this tilt again when we learn about the seasons.
Have you seen a **lattu** spin?
We also call it a top.
It spins round and round in one place.
Earth spins like a top, on its own tilted axis.
This spinning on its axis is Earth's **rotation**.
Earth always spins in one direction, from **west to east**.
You know east and west from the chapter on map reading.

visual.title: Spinning Like a Top
visual.description: A lattu spinning round its upright axis beside Earth spinning round its slightly tilted axis, from west to east: rotation.

question.prompt: Earth's spinning on its own axis is called ___.

options.text: revolution
tilt
rotation

hint.display: Think of the lattu spinning in one place.

grading.correctAnswerText: rotation
grading.reason: Yes! Earth's spinning on its axis is its rotation.

question.prompt: Arjun says Earth's axis is a real stick. Which of these show the axis is imaginary?

options.text: A spinning bangle turns around its empty middle.
A spinning thing needs a real stick inside it.
A ball spinning on a table has no stick inside.
We can touch the line in a bangle's middle.

hint.display: Think about what is in the middle of a spinning bangle.

grading.correctAnswerText: A spinning bangle turns around its empty middle.; A ball spinning on a table has no stick inside.
grading.reason: Great thinking! Earth's axis is imaginary, like the line through the bangle.

lines.display: Let's make a model to see rotation.
Take an orange: this is our Earth.
With an adult's help, push a knitting needle down through its middle.
Tilt the needle a little, like Earth's axis.
Now turn the orange slowly on the needle.
That turning is **rotation**!

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: An Orange Model

lines.display: Does Earth have a real rod through it, like this needle?
No, it does not.
The needle is only there to hold the orange.
It shows us where the axis is.
A classroom globe has a rod for the same reason.
The real Earth has no rod.
Its axis is **imaginary**, like the line through the bangle's empty middle.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: No Real Rod

cards.title: Day and Night on the Orange

lines.display: Now let's see how rotation gives us day and night.
Take the orange into a dark room.
Switch on a lamp.
The lamp is our Sun.
Hold the orange in front of the lamp.

conceptGroup.goal: See how Earth's spin gives us day and night
conceptGroup.title: Day and night on the orange

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Day and Night on the Orange

lines.display: Look at the orange.
The half facing the lamp is bright.
That half has **day**.
The other half, away from the lamp, is dark.
That half has **night**.

conceptGroup.goal: See how Earth's spin gives us day and night
conceptGroup.title: Day and night on the orange

visual.title: Half Bright, Half Dark
visual.description: An orange in front of a lamp in a dark room: the half facing the lamp is bright (day), the half away from it is dark (night).

interactive.label: Turn the orange in front of the lamp

lines.display: It is the same on Earth.
The half of Earth facing the Sun has day.
The other half has night.
So the whole Earth never has day at the same time.
And the whole Earth never has night at the same time.

conceptGroup.goal: See how Earth's spin gives us day and night
conceptGroup.title: Day and night on the orange

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: The Same on Earth

lines.display: Now stick a bindi or a small paper dot on the orange.
This dot is you, in India.
Turn the orange slowly, always the same way.
First, the dot comes into the light: morning, then day.
Next, it moves round into the dark: night.
Then it comes back into the light: the next morning!
This happens again and again.

conceptGroup.goal: See how Earth's spin gives us day and night
conceptGroup.title: Day and night on the orange

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: A Dot for You

question.prompt:
True or false?

Right now, some part of Earth has night.

options.text: True
False

hint.display: Think about the half of Earth facing away from the Sun.

grading.correctAnswerText: True
grading.reason: Yes, it is true! The half facing away from the Sun has night.

conceptGroup.goal: See how Earth's spin gives us day and night
conceptGroup.title: Day and night on the orange

question.prompt: The dot is in the dark now. You keep turning the orange the same way. Which of these are true?

options.text: The lamp has stopped shining.
The dot will stay in the dark forever.
The dot has night.
The half facing the lamp has day.
The dot will come back into the light.

hint.display: Picture the dot going round as you turn the orange.

grading.correctAnswerText: The dot has night.; The half facing the lamp has day.; The dot will come back into the light.
grading.reason: Well done! The dot keeps moving from night into day, again and again.

conceptGroup.goal: See how Earth's spin gives us day and night
conceptGroup.title: Day and night on the orange

lines.display: You might think the Sun goes away at night.
Or you might think it goes round to the other side.
But look at the lamp.
It never moved, and its light never went away.
The dot sat in the dark for a while.
All that time, the lamp was shining on the other half.

conceptGroup.goal: See how Earth's spin gives us day and night
conceptGroup.title: Day and night on the orange

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: The Lamp Never Moved

lines.display: It is the same with the real Sun.
The Sun is not going round us.
**Earth is turning.**
While one side of Earth has night, the other side has day.

conceptGroup.goal: See how Earth's spin gives us day and night
conceptGroup.title: Day and night on the orange

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Earth Is Turning

cards.title: Night in India, Day in America

lines.display: America is very far from India.
It is on the other side of Earth.
So when it is night in India, it is day in America.
Suppose you video-call a relative in America at bedtime.
You will see sunshine behind them!
A torch shining on a globe in a dark room shows this too.
When India is on the dark side, America is in the light.

conceptGroup.goal: See how Earth's spin gives us day and night
conceptGroup.title: Day and night on the orange

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Night in India, Day in America

lines.display: How long does one full spin take?
Turn the orange once, all the way round.
The dot goes from morning, through day and night, to the next morning.
One full turn gives one day and one night.
You already know that one day and one night together make 24 hours.
So Earth takes **24 hours** to spin once.

conceptGroup.goal: See how Earth's spin gives us day and night
conceptGroup.title: Day and night on the orange

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: One Full Spin

cards.title: Rotation Gives Us Day and Night

lines.display: So **rotation** is Earth spinning on its own axis, from west to east.
The half facing the Sun has day, and the other half has night.
As Earth spins, each place moves from day into night, and back again.
One full spin takes 24 hours.
That is how rotation gives us **day and night**.

conceptGroup.goal: See how Earth's spin gives us day and night
conceptGroup.title: Day and night on the orange

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Rotation Gives Us Day and Night

24 hours
one week

conceptGroup.goal: See how Earth's spin gives us day and night
conceptGroup.title: Day and night on the orange

options.text: Earth is turning, and India faces away from the Sun.
The Sun goes away from India at night.
The Sun moves round to America.

hint.display: Remember the lamp: it never moved.

grading.correctAnswerText: Earth is turning, and India faces away from the Sun.
grading.reason: Great thinking! Earth is turning, and the Sun never goes away.

lines.display: Earth's spinning does something else too.
It makes shadows move!
Long ago, there were no clocks or watches.
So people used moving shadows to tell the time.
They used a **sundial**, the old clock that reads the Sun's shadow.
Let's see how a sundial works.

conceptGroup.goal: See how a sundial uses a shadow to show the time
conceptGroup.title: How a sundial tells the time

visual.title: Shadows That Tell the Time
visual.description: One sundial built up stage by stage: the Sun and a flat dial, the upright gnomon, its shadow and the shadow's later positions, and the hour marks 3, 12 and 9, with the shadow falling on 9.

lines.display: A sundial has a flat surface.
An **upright** stick stands at its centre.
**Upright** means standing straight up.
We call this stick the **gnomon**.
The g is silent, so we say it “no-mon”.

conceptGroup.goal: See how a sundial uses a shadow to show the time
conceptGroup.title: How a sundial tells the time

visual.title: Shadows That Tell the Time
visual.description: One sundial built up stage by stage: the Sun and a flat dial, the upright gnomon, its shadow and the shadow's later positions, and the hour marks 3, 12 and 9, with the shadow falling on 9.

lines.display: The Sun shines on the gnomon.
So the gnomon makes a shadow on the flat surface.
Through the day, this shadow moves to new **positions**.
A **position** is the place where something is.

conceptGroup.goal: See how a sundial uses a shadow to show the time
conceptGroup.title: How a sundial tells the time

visual.title: Shadows That Tell the Time
visual.description: One sundial built up stage by stage: the Sun and a flat dial, the upright gnomon, its shadow and the shadow's later positions, and the hour marks 3, 12 and 9, with the shadow falling on 9.

lines.display: A sundial has a mark for each position of the shadow.
Each mark shows a time.
To read the time, see which mark the shadow falls on.

conceptGroup.goal: See how a sundial uses a shadow to show the time
conceptGroup.title: How a sundial tells the time

visual.title: Shadows That Tell the Time
visual.description: One sundial built up stage by stage: the Sun and a flat dial, the upright gnomon, its shadow and the shadow's later positions, and the hour marks 3, 12 and 9, with the shadow falling on 9.

lines.display: A sundial needs sunshine.
No sunshine means no shadow.
And no shadow means no time to read.
So a sundial cannot work at **night**.
It cannot work when **clouds** cover the Sun either.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: No Sun, No Time

lines.display: People used sundials in many countries.
People in India used them too.
Some still stand at old temples and other old, famous places.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Sundials Everywhere

lines.display: The biggest stone sundial in the world is in India!
Its name is the **Samrat Yantra**.
It stands at **Jantar Mantar** in Jaipur, Rajasthan.
**Maharaja Sawai Jai Singh II** got it built in the 18th century.
That means the 1700s, nearly 300 years ago.
It tells the time very well.
It can be wrong by about 2 seconds, but not more!

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: The Samrat Yantra

question.prompt:
True or false?

The biggest stone sundial in the world is in India.

options.text: True
False

hint.display: Think of the Samrat Yantra and where it stands.

grading.correctAnswerText: True
grading.reason: Yes, it is true! The Samrat Yantra in Jaipur is the biggest one.

question.prompt: Meera wants to read the time on her sundial. Which of these are true?

options.text: She needs sunshine.
She looks at which mark the shadow falls on.
She can read it at night.
She needs the shadow of the gnomon.
She can read it when clouds cover the Sun.

hint.display: Remember: no sunshine means no shadow.

grading.correctAnswerText: She needs sunshine.; She looks at which mark the shadow falls on.; She needs the shadow of the gnomon.
grading.reason: Well done! A sundial needs sunshine, so it cannot work at night.

lines.display: Now let's watch how a shadow changes through a sunny day.
Push a stick into the ground, so it stands upright.
A gnomon is just a stick like this.
Put a small stone at the tip of the stick's shadow.
The stone marks where the shadow ends.

conceptGroup.goal: Watch how a stick's shadow changes through a sunny day
conceptGroup.title: Watch a stick's shadow

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Watch a Shadow Change

lines.display: Come back after one hour and look again.
Compare the new shadow with your stone.
The shadow is now a different **size**.
Size here means how long it is.
The shadow also points a different way.
Look again every hour: the shadow keeps changing.

conceptGroup.goal: Watch how a stick's shadow changes through a sunny day
conceptGroup.title: Watch a stick's shadow

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: One Hour Later

lines.display: So a shadow changes in **two ways** through the day.
Its **size** changes.
And its **direction** changes too.

conceptGroup.goal: Watch how a stick's shadow changes through a sunny day
conceptGroup.title: Watch a stick's shadow

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Two Ways a Shadow Changes

cards.title: Shortest When the Sun Is Highest

lines.display: Notice one more thing.
The shadow is **shortest** when the Sun is **highest** in the sky.
When the Sun is low, the shadow is long.
Think of your own shadow in the evening.
The Sun is low then, and your shadow is very long!

conceptGroup.goal: Watch how a stick's shadow changes through a sunny day
conceptGroup.title: Watch a stick's shadow

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Shortest When the Sun Is Highest

question.prompt: When is a stick's shadow shortest?

options.text: When the Sun is low in the sky
In the evening
When the Sun is highest in the sky

hint.display: Think of your own long shadow in the evening.

grading.correctAnswerText: When the Sun is highest in the sky
grading.reason: Yes! The shadow is shortest when the Sun is highest.

conceptGroup.goal: Watch how a stick's shadow changes through a sunny day
conceptGroup.title: Watch a stick's shadow

question.prompt: Aarav puts a stone at the tip of a stick's shadow. One hour later, he looks again. Which of these are true now?

options.text: The shadow has not changed at all.
Only the size changed, not the way it points.
The shadow is a different size.
The shadow points a different way.

hint.display: Compare the new shadow with the stone.

grading.correctAnswerText: The shadow is a different size.; The shadow points a different way.
grading.reason: Great thinking! A shadow changes in two ways: its size and its direction.

conceptGroup.goal: Watch how a stick's shadow changes through a sunny day
conceptGroup.title: Watch a stick's shadow

lines.display: Why do shadows move like this?
Let's go back to the orange and the lamp.
Remember, the lamp never moved.
Only the orange turned.

conceptGroup.goal: Find out why shadows move through the day
conceptGroup.title: Why shadows move

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Why Do Shadows Move?

lines.display: Imagine you are the dot on the orange.
As the orange turns, you turn with it.
So you see the lamp from a new place.
First the lamp looks low in your sky.
Then it looks high, and then low again.
The lamp never moved, but you did!

conceptGroup.goal: Find out why shadows move through the day
conceptGroup.title: Why shadows move

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Be the Dot

lines.display: It is the same with Earth and the Sun.
As Earth turns, the Sun's place in our sky changes.
In the morning, the Sun looks low.
Later in the day, it looks high.
In the evening, it looks low again.
So the Sun **seems** to travel across our sky.

conceptGroup.goal: Find out why shadows move through the day
conceptGroup.title: Why shadows move

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: The Sun Seems to Travel

lines.display: But the Sun only seems to make this trip.
**Earth** is the one that really moves.
A shadow always falls on the side away from the Sun.
So when the Sun's place in our sky changes, every shadow moves too.
That is why a sundial's shadow can show the time.

conceptGroup.goal: Find out why shadows move through the day
conceptGroup.title: Why shadows move

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Why Shadows Move

lines.display: Here is a puzzle.
If Earth is spinning, why don't we feel it?
Think of a ride on a train.
When the train runs smoothly, close your eyes.
You cannot tell that you are moving.
You feel the train only when it bumps, starts or stops.

conceptGroup.goal: Find out why we cannot feel Earth spinning
conceptGroup.title: Why we don't feel Earth spin

visual.title: A Smooth Train Ride
visual.description: The same train twice: on a smooth track a passenger with closed eyes cannot tell it is moving; on a bump the jolt is felt.

lines.display: Now open your eyes.
Look at a cup of chai on the train's table.
It does not spill.
Why not?
It moves along with you and the train.

conceptGroup.goal: Find out why we cannot feel Earth spinning
conceptGroup.title: Why we don't feel Earth spin

visual.title: The Cup of Chai
visual.description: Inside the moving train, a cup of chai on the table stays level because it moves along with the train: two arrows pointing the same way.

lines.display: Then look out of the window.
The trees and poles seem to rush backwards.
But the trees are not moving.
You are!

conceptGroup.goal: Find out why we cannot feel Earth spinning
conceptGroup.title: Why we don't feel Earth spin

visual.title: Out of the Window
visual.description: From the train window the trees and poles seem to rush backwards, while outside they stand still and only the train moves.

lines.display: Earth carries us the same way.
But Earth is even smoother than a train.
It carries us, the air and everything else along with it.
It never bumps, and it never stops.
So we feel nothing at all.
And the Sun seems to move, just like the trees outside the train.

conceptGroup.goal: Find out why we cannot feel Earth spinning
conceptGroup.title: Why we don't feel Earth spin

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Earth Carries Us

question.prompt:
True or false?

We can feel Earth spinning.

options.text: True
False

hint.display: Think of the chai on the smooth train.

grading.correctAnswerText: False
grading.reason: Right, it is false! Earth is spinning, but we feel nothing at all.

conceptGroup.goal: Find out why we cannot feel Earth spinning
conceptGroup.title: Why we don't feel Earth spin

question.prompt: From a train, trees seem to rush backwards. What does this tell us about the Sun crossing our sky?

options.text: The Sun really moves across our sky.
The Sun only seems to move, because Earth is turning.
Earth is not moving at all.

hint.display: Ask: are the trees really moving, or are you?

grading.correctAnswerText: The Sun only seems to move, because Earth is turning.
grading.reason: Great thinking! Like the trees, the Sun only seems to move.

conceptGroup.goal: Find out why we cannot feel Earth spinning
conceptGroup.title: Why we don't feel Earth spin

lines.display: Earth does one more thing that we cannot feel.
While Earth spins, it also travels around the Sun.
Let's go back to our orange and lamp.

conceptGroup.goal: See how Earth travels around the Sun, and how long one trip takes
conceptGroup.title: Earth's trip around the Sun

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Earth's Trip Around the Sun

lines.display: Keep turning the orange on its tilted needle.
At the same time, carry it slowly all the way around the lamp.
Then go around again, along the same path.
We call Earth's path around the Sun its **orbit**.
Earth's orbit stays the same, year after year.

conceptGroup.goal: See how Earth travels around the Sun, and how long one trip takes
conceptGroup.title: Earth's trip around the Sun

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Earth's Orbit

lines.display: Earth **revolves** around the Sun.
To **revolve** means to go around something.
One full trip around the Sun is one **revolution**.
It takes **one year**.
That is about 365 days, from one birthday to the next!

conceptGroup.goal: See how Earth travels around the Sun, and how long one trip takes
conceptGroup.title: Earth's trip around the Sun

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: One Revolution, One Year

lines.display: Remember, one spin takes 24 hours.
That is one day and one night together.
A year has about 365 days and nights.
So during one trip around the Sun, Earth spins about 365 times!

conceptGroup.goal: See how Earth travels around the Sun, and how long one trip takes
conceptGroup.title: Earth's trip around the Sun

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: 365 Spins in One Trip

lines.display: Now we have three words.
The **orbit** is the path.
A **revolution** is one full trip along the path.
And to **revolve** is to go around.

conceptGroup.goal: See how Earth travels around the Sun, and how long one trip takes
conceptGroup.title: Earth's trip around the Sun

question.prompt: Earth's path around the Sun is called its ___.

options.text: orbit
revolution
axis

hint.display: Remember the orange going round the lamp on the same path.

grading.correctAnswerText: orbit
grading.reason: Yes! The orbit is the path Earth travels around the Sun.

conceptGroup.goal: See how Earth travels around the Sun, and how long one trip takes
conceptGroup.title: Earth's trip around the Sun

question.prompt: Kabir says Earth stops spinning while it goes around the Sun. Which of these show he is wrong?

options.text: Earth spins only once in a whole year.
Earth spins about 365 times in one trip.
The orange stopped turning as it went round the lamp.
Day and night stop while Earth travels around the Sun.
We get day and night all through the year.

hint.display: Remember: each day and night comes from one spin.

grading.correctAnswerText: Earth spins about 365 times in one trip.; We get day and night all through the year.
grading.reason: Great thinking! Earth keeps spinning, about 365 times in each trip.

conceptGroup.goal: See how Earth travels around the Sun, and how long one trip takes
conceptGroup.title: Earth's trip around the Sun

lines.display: Remember the tilt of Earth's axis?
Earth travels around the Sun with this tilt.
As it does, the seasons change through the year.
We get **spring**, **summer**, **autumn** and **winter**.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: The Seasons

lines.display: Two things bring the seasons, and they work together.
One is Earth's trip around the Sun.
The other is the tilt of its axis.
The seasons need **both**.
One alone is not enough.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Two Things Together

lines.display: You might think summer comes when Earth is nearer the Sun.
You might think winter comes when it is farther away.
Many grown-ups think so too.
But let's check if this is true.

conceptGroup.goal: Test if summer comes from Earth being nearer the Sun
conceptGroup.title: Is summer about being nearer the Sun?

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Nearer the Sun?

lines.display: In December and January, it is winter in India.
These are our coolest months.
On those very same days, it is summer in Australia!
Think of a cricket match in Australia in December or January.
The players play in hot, bright sunshine.
The crowds wear caps and sunglasses.
And children there are on their summer holidays.

conceptGroup.goal: Test if summer comes from Earth being nearer the Sun
conceptGroup.title: Is summer about being nearer the Sun?

lines.display: India and Australia are on the same Earth.
On those days, both are the same distance from the Sun.
But India has winter, and Australia has summer.
So summer does not come from being nearer the Sun.
And winter does not come from being farther away.

conceptGroup.goal: Test if summer comes from Earth being nearer the Sun
conceptGroup.title: Is summer about being nearer the Sun?

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: The Same Distance

lines.display: So what makes their seasons different?
It is the **tilt** of Earth's axis.
The tilt gives different parts of Earth different seasons at the same time.
When the top half of Earth has summer, the bottom half has winter.
And when the bottom half has summer, the top half has winter.

conceptGroup.goal: Test if summer comes from Earth being nearer the Sun
conceptGroup.title: Is summer about being nearer the Sun?

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: It Is the Tilt

lines.display: Let's put it all together.
On the same days, India has winter and Australia has summer.
Both are the same distance from the Sun.
India is in the top half of Earth.
Australia is in the bottom half.
Because of the tilt, their seasons are **opposite**.

conceptGroup.goal: Test if summer comes from Earth being nearer the Sun
conceptGroup.title: Is summer about being nearer the Sun?

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Opposite Seasons

question.prompt:
True or false?

When India has winter, Australia has winter too.

options.text: True
False

hint.display: Think of the cricket match in Australia in December.

grading.correctAnswerText: False
grading.reason: Right, it is false! When India has winter, Australia has summer.

conceptGroup.goal: Test if summer comes from Earth being nearer the Sun
conceptGroup.title: Is summer about being nearer the Sun?

question.prompt: In January, India has winter and Australia has summer. Why?

options.text: Australia is nearer the Sun than India.
The Sun goes away from India in January.
The tilt of Earth's axis gives them different seasons.

hint.display: Remember: both are the same distance from the Sun.

grading.correctAnswerText: The tilt of Earth's axis gives them different seasons.
grading.reason: Great thinking! Because of the tilt, India and Australia have opposite seasons.

conceptGroup.goal: Test if summer comes from Earth being nearer the Sun
conceptGroup.title: Is summer about being nearer the Sun?

lines.display: Now let's put Earth's two movements next to each other.
**Rotation** is Earth spinning on its axis.
It takes 24 hours.
It gives us day and night.
**Revolution** is Earth's trip around the Sun.
It takes one year.
Together with the tilt, it gives us the seasons.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Two Movements Side by Side

lines.display: Here is a trick, so you always know which movement does which job.
Ask: how often does it come back?
Let's try it on day and night, and then on the seasons.

conceptGroup.goal: Match day and night, and the seasons, to the right movement
conceptGroup.title: Which movement does which job?

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: A Trick to Remember

lines.display: Day and night come back every single day.
From one birthday to the next, you have about 365 nights.
So day and night must come from the one-day movement.
That is the spin: **rotation**.

conceptGroup.goal: Match day and night, and the seasons, to the right movement
conceptGroup.title: Which movement does which job?

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Every Single Day

lines.display: Summer comes back only once a year.
From one birthday to the next, you have just one summer.
So the seasons must come from the one-year movement, together with the tilt.
That movement is the trip around the Sun: **revolution**.
And during that one trip, Earth spins about 365 times.

conceptGroup.goal: Match day and night, and the seasons, to the right movement
conceptGroup.title: Which movement does which job?

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Only Once a Year

question.prompt: Count from one birthday to the next. You have about 365 ___.

options.text: nights
summers
years

hint.display: Day and night come back every single day.

grading.correctAnswerText: nights
grading.reason: Yes! You have about 365 nights, but just one summer.

conceptGroup.goal: Match day and night, and the seasons, to the right movement
conceptGroup.title: Which movement does which job?

question.prompt: Which of these are true about Earth's two movements?

options.text: Rotation gives us day and night.
Revolution, with the tilt, gives us the seasons.
Rotation gives us the seasons.
Revolution gives us day and night.

hint.display: Ask: how often does it come back?

grading.correctAnswerText: Rotation gives us day and night.; Revolution, with the tilt, gives us the seasons.
grading.reason: Well done! Day and night come from rotation, seasons from revolution and tilt.

conceptGroup.goal: Match day and night, and the seasons, to the right movement
conceptGroup.title: Which movement does which job?

lines.display: Look how much you now know about our Earth!
Water covers most of Earth's surface.
Out of every 100 parts, 71 are water and 29 are land.
Earth is the third planet from the Sun.
It is at the right distance from the Sun.
A layer of air covers it.
So it is a good home for life.
Earth is round like a ball, but a little squashed.
We call this shape an **oblate spheroid**.
Earth spins on its axis once every 24 hours.
This **rotation** gives us day and night.
It also makes shadows move, so a sundial can tell the time.
Earth also travels around the Sun once a year.
This **revolution**, together with the tilt, gives us the seasons.
Now you can explain why we have day and night.
And you can explain why the seasons change.
Well done!
